newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa's Tutu piles pressure on ruling ANC.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa's Tutu piles pressure on ruling ANC.

text.p: Nobel peace laureate Desmond Tutu on Monday threatened to resign from South Africa's Truth and Reconciliation Commission if the ruling African National Congress refused to seek amnesty for past human rights abuses.

Tutu, widely regarded as the country's moral conscience, piled pressure onto President Nelson Mandela's ANC, insisting publicly that it could not unilaterally declare itself blameless in the fight against white rule.
"If this position is accepted as ANC policy, we will then have to look for another chairperson," a straight-talking Tutu told reporters in the Indian Ocean port city of Durban.

Tutu lambasted the ANC's chief legal adviser, Mathews Phosa, for saying former ANC guerrillas did not need to ask for amnesty for bombings, shootings and other killings because their fight against apartheid was a "just struggle".
"There is no crisis yet but it will become a crisis should the ANC decide it wants to adopt that particular position.
"If we allow the ANC...to get away with it, then people will justifiably say that the commission is a witch hunt by looking for people from only one side," the former Anglican archbishop said.

Tutu said he hoped the ANC would adopt a clear position stating that its members and leaders would apply to the truth commission for amnesty for any act in respect of which they might be liable for prosecution or civil damages.
He added Mandela had informed him at a private meeting on Friday that the party would make a final decision on amnesty this week.
Revelations before the truth commission so far have shown that the extra-judicial killing of government opponents during the 1980s was state-sanctioned, and not confined to renegade police units.

But tension is building over the failure of any individual ANC member to approach the commission for amnesty, even for those human rights abuses committed by the liberation movement against its own members during its years in exile.
An ANC-appointed inquiry in the early 1990s found 22 ANC members were executed or allowed to die through starvation or neglect in camps in Angola, Zambia, Tanzania and Uganda.

ANC leaders say the atrocities have to be seen in the wider context of the apartheid war, and have accused former white governments of responsibility for the deaths in detention of 73 political prisoners and assassination of about 220 activists.
But the National Party, which implemented apartheid in 1948 and began dismantling it in 1990, has criticised the ANC's attitude saying it does not bode well for reconciliation.
"Individuals who have committed criminal acts or acts which infringe human rights, for whatever political cause, must face the consequences of those acts," the party said.

White parties to the right of the National Party have said the failure of ANC members to seek amnesty for killing civilians during their armed struggle confirmed their belief the truth commission was biased against the apartheid security forces.
